title: Acute chest pain in general practice: cardiovascular examination
desc: This station involves a focused chest pain history and a full cardiovascular examination of a 60-year-old smoker with acute central chest pain in a general practice clinic, then reading his observations and 12-lead ECG, recognising an acute anterolateral STEMI, and starting immediate management (000, aspirin, GTN, IV access, analgesia, monitoring) while arranging reperfusion.
focus: Cardiovascular examination in acute chest pain, and immediate management of STEMI in general practice
stem: You are a final-year medical student on placement at a general practice clinic. Phillip, a 60-year-old accountant, has walked in complaining of acute chest pain. His wife drove him here. The practice nurse has taken his observations, settled him on the examination couch and is setting up to record a 12-lead ECG. Your supervising GP is in the building and has asked you to see Phillip straight away.
tasks: Take a focused history from Phillip and perform a focused cardiovascular examination, telling the examiner what you are examining and why (10 minutes).
The examiner will give you Phillip's observations and his 12-lead ECG. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and your safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Phillip, a 60-year-old accountant. You are in obvious pain, a little grey and sweaty, and you keep rubbing the middle of your chest. You talk in short sentences but can answer questions. You are trying not to make a fuss. The examiner gives examination findings from the Exam findings below when the candidate says what they are examining.

Opening line: "I've got this terrible pain in my chest. It came on about three-quarters of an hour ago and it just won't go away."

The pain (give only when asked):

  • Onset: came on over a minute or two about 45 minutes ago while you were sitting at your desk at home doing paperwork. You were not exerting yourself.
  • Site and radiation: right in the middle of the chest, behind the breastbone. It goes down the inside of your left arm and up into your jaw.
  • Character: heavy and crushing, "like someone sitting on my chest". Not sharp, not stabbing, not tearing.
  • Severity: 8 out of 10, the worst pain you have ever had.
  • Course: constant since it started. Sitting still has not helped. Two antacid tablets did nothing.
  • Aggravating: not worse with breathing in, moving, pressing on the chest or lying down. Not better sitting forward.
  • Back: no pain going through to the back or between the shoulder blades.

Associated symptoms: you broke out in a sweat and felt sick when it started, but have not vomited. You feel a bit short of breath. No palpitations. You feel a little light-headed but have not fainted. No weakness, numbness, change in speech or vision.

Previous episodes (only if asked): for the last two weeks you have had a tightness in the chest when walking up the two flights of stairs to your office. It went away within a couple of minutes of stopping. You put it down to being unfit and did not mention it to anyone. You have never had pain like today's.

Other causes (only if asked): no cough, fever, haemoptysis or recent cold. No calf pain or leg swelling. No recent long flights, car trips, surgery or time in bed. No heartburn history.

Past medical history: high blood pressure and high cholesterol for about 8 years. No diabetes. No previous heart attack, angina diagnosis, stroke, stomach ulcer or bleeding problems. No recent operations or injuries.

Medicines: ramipril (for blood pressure) and atorvastatin (for cholesterol), taken every morning. You do not take aspirin or blood thinners. You have never used erectile dysfunction tablets (sildenafil, Viagra, Cialis). No over-the-counter medicines apart from the antacid today. No known allergies, including to aspirin.

Family history: your father had a heart attack in his 70s. No sudden deaths in the family.

Social history: you live at home with your wife, Margaret, who drove you here (the practice is five minutes from home) and is in the waiting room. You work as an accountant, mostly from home at the moment. You have smoked a pack a day for the last 30 years and have never seriously tried to stop. About six beers over a weekend. No recreational drugs.

Ideas, concerns, expectations: you hope it is indigestion or a pulled muscle. Underneath, you are frightened it is your heart, like your father. You did not want to "make a fuss" by calling an ambulance. You expect to be given something for the pain and to go home.

How you change: if the candidate arranges a GTN spray during Part 1, the pain eases a little to 6 out of 10 but does not go away. Otherwise it stays at 8 out of 10. If the candidate asks for an ECG, the examiner says: "The nurse is recording it now. You will see it in Part 2."

Exam findings (the examiner gives these only when the candidate examines that area)

  • General inspection: overweight man (92 kg, 176 cm) lying at 45 degrees, in pain, pale and sweaty, mildly short of breath while talking. Not cachectic, no oedema. No features of Marfan syndrome or other syndromes.
  • Vital signs: heart rate 96 beats/min, regular. Blood pressure 152/90 mmHg right arm, 148/88 mmHg left arm. If the candidate mentions or starts to take the following, stop them and give: respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.7 °C.
  • Pulses: radial pulse 96 regular, normal volume and character. No radio-radial delay. No radio-femoral delay. Femoral pulses equal.
  • Hands: cool and clammy. Tar staining of the right index and middle fingers. Capillary refill 2 seconds. No clubbing, splinter haemorrhages, Osler's nodes, Janeway lesions, peripheral cyanosis or tendon xanthomata.
  • Eyes: bilateral corneal arcus. No xanthelasma. No conjunctival pallor. Pupils equal and reactive.
  • Mouth and face: no central cyanosis. Teeth in fair condition, no obvious decay. Normal palate. No malar flush.
  • Neck: carotid pulses normal volume and character, no bruits. JVP 2 cm above the sternal angle (not raised).
  • Praecordium inspection: no scars, no pacemaker, no visible pulsations, no chest wall deformity.
  • Palpation: apex beat in the 5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line, not displaced, normal character. No heaves. No thrills. No chest wall tenderness.
  • Auscultation: S1 and S2 heard in all areas, dual. No added sounds (no S3). No murmurs, including sitting forward in expiration and in the left lateral position. No pericardial rub.
  • Lungs: resonant to percussion, vesicular breath sounds, no crackles or wheeze at the bases.
  • Abdomen: soft, non-tender. No hepatomegaly or splenomegaly. No pulsatile mass, no aortic bruit. No ascites.
  • Lower limbs: no pitting oedema. Peripheral pulses present. No calf tenderness or swelling. No Achilles tendon xanthomata. Normal hair distribution, no pallor, no clubbing of the toes.

check.x: Professionalism

Hand hygiene, introduces self (name and role), confirms the patient's identity, gains consent for the examination, offers a chaperone, exposes to the waist with dignity and positions him at 45 degrees.
Notices his pain and distress at the outset, keeps him resting on the couch, explains each step in plain language and keeps the history brief and targeted because this may be an emergency.
History
Characterises the chest pain:

kids.x: Onset and what he was doing: came on over minutes, at rest, about 45 minutes ago.
Site and radiation: central, retrosternal, to the left arm and jaw.
Course and modifying factors: constant, not relieved by rest or antacid, not pleuritic, positional or reproduced by pressing.

check.x: Asks about associated symptoms: sweating, nausea or vomiting, breathlessness, palpitations, light-headedness or fainting.
Asks about previous episodes and finds two weeks of chest tightness on climbing stairs that settled with rest.
Screens for other serious causes of chest pain:

kids.x: Aortic dissection: sudden tearing pain through to the back, neurological symptoms.
Pulmonary embolism: pleuritic pain, haemoptysis, calf swelling, recent travel, surgery or immobility.
Pericarditis and others: pain worse lying flat or eased sitting forward, recent viral illness; reflux symptoms.

check.x: Takes the cardiovascular risk factors: quantifies smoking (a pack a day for 30 years, 30 pack-years), hypertension and cholesterol, diabetes, and family history of heart disease.
Takes medicines and allergies, and checks for contraindications to acute treatment:

kids.x: Current medicines (ramipril, atorvastatin) and allergies, including to aspirin.
Recent use of a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor (sildenafil or vardenafil within 24 hours, tadalafil within 48 hours), which contraindicates GTN.
Bleeding risk: peptic ulcer or bleeding, anticoagulants, recent surgery or stroke.

check.x: Asks the social history (lives with his wife, who drove him in; occupation; alcohol; recreational drugs such as cocaine or amphetamines) and explores his ideas, concerns and expectations (hopes it is indigestion, fears a heart attack like his father, did not want to call an ambulance).
Examination
General inspection: pain, distress, pallor and sweating, breathlessness, body habitus, cachexia, oedema, and features of Marfan syndrome or other syndromes.
Takes heart rate and blood pressure in both arms (looking for an inter-arm difference that suggests dissection), and asks for respiratory rate, oxygen saturation and temperature.
Examines the pulses: radial rate and rhythm, radio-radial delay and radio-femoral delay.
Examines the hands: temperature and capillary refill, tar staining, clubbing, splinter haemorrhages, Osler's nodes, Janeway lesions, peripheral cyanosis and tendon xanthomata.
Examines the eyes, mouth and face: conjunctival pallor, corneal arcus, xanthelasma, central cyanosis, dental decay, high-arched palate and malar flush.
Examines the neck: carotid pulse volume and character, carotid bruits, and the height of the JVP.

Inspects and palpates the praecordium: scars, pacemaker, visible pulsations; locates the apex beat (5th intercostal space, mid-clavicular line); feels for heaves at the left parasternal edge and thrills over each valve area.
Auscultates the heart:

kids.x: Listens over all four valve areas, commenting on S1 and S2, added sounds, murmurs and a pericardial rub.
Uses manoeuvres: sitting forward in expiration for the aortic and pulmonary areas, left lateral position for the mitral area, left-sided sounds in expiration and right-sided in inspiration.
States what matters in this patient: a new murmur (mitral regurgitation from a complication of infarction, aortic regurgitation from dissection), a third heart sound or a rub.

check.x: Completes the examination or states they would: lung bases (crackles, effusion), abdomen (liver, spleen, abdominal aorta, ascites) and lower limbs (pitting oedema, pulses, Achilles xanthomata, hair loss, pallor, clubbing of the toes).
Asks for, or confirms and prioritises, the 12-lead ECG straight away (within 10 minutes of arrival) and asks to see it as soon as it is recorded, not after finishing the examination.
Interpretation

Interprets the observations: heart rate rising from 96 to 104 (now mildly tachycardic), blood pressure raised but well above 90 mmHg systolic with no significant inter-arm difference, SpO2 96 to 97% on room air, mildly raised respiratory rate, afebrile, ongoing pain (8/10, or 6/10 after GTN); not shocked and no heart failure on examination (clear lungs, no S3, JVP not raised: Killip class I), but worsening without treatment.

Reads the ECG systematically: sinus rhythm at 98, normal axis and intervals, ST elevation in V1 to V5, I and aVL meeting STEMI criteria, reciprocal ST depression in III and aVF, hyperacute T waves, and new compared with the ECG from 2 years ago.

States the diagnosis: acute anterolateral ST-elevation myocardial infarction (probably a proximal left anterior descending artery occlusion), within 12 hours of onset, so he needs urgent reperfusion; and considers and rejects aortic dissection (no tearing back pain, equal arm pressures and pulses, no aortic regurgitation murmur) and pericarditis (territorial ST elevation with reciprocal change, no PR depression).
Management
Recognises a time-critical emergency in a general practice clinic:

kids.x: Calls 000 straight away, states that the ECG shows a STEMI and asks for an urgent ambulance.
Does not let his wife drive him or send him to ED by private car, and does not wait for a troponin or other blood results.

check.x: Gives aspirin 300 mg orally (chewed or dissolved) after confirming he has no allergy.

Gives GTN 1 to 2 sprays (400 to 800 micrograms) under the tongue, repeated every 5 minutes if pain persists, up to 3 doses, provided systolic BP stays at least 90 mmHg and he has taken no PDE5 inhibitor (sildenafil/vardenafil within 24 h, tadalafil within 48 h).
Gives oxygen only if SpO2 is below 93% (NHFA/CSANZ), and states he does not need it at 96 to 97% on room air.
check.d: Accept either threshold (93% NHFA/CSANZ, or 90% ESC) when marking.

check.x: Inserts two large-bore IV cannulae, taking bloods at the same time without delaying transfer.

For severe pain that continues, gives IV opioid titrated to effect: morphine 2.5 to 5 mg every 5 to 10 minutes or fentanyl 25 to 50 micrograms every 5 to 10 minutes, watching blood pressure and breathing.
Stays with him with continuous monitoring and repeat observations, keeps the defibrillator beside him, and is ready to start CPR and defibrillate if he arrests (ventricular fibrillation).

States the definitive plan: urgent reperfusion, with primary PCI at a cardiac catheter laboratory, or fibrinolysis if PCI cannot be delivered in time, decided with the paramedics and the receiving cardiology team.
Hands over the ECGs, drugs given with times, and onset time to the paramedics.

Tells Phillip honestly and in plain words that this is a heart attack caused by a blocked artery, that the ambulance will take him to hospital to have it opened, and why Margaret cannot drive him. Brings Margaret in and checks understanding.
Safety netting

While waiting for the ambulance, tells Phillip to say straight away if the pain gets worse or he becomes more breathless, faint or has palpitations, and briefs the nurse to start CPR and use the defibrillator if he collapses.

Outlines the plan after discharge: a written heart attack action plan (call 000, never drive, if chest pain is severe, gets worse quickly or lasts more than 10 minutes), GP review with the discharge summary, cardiac rehabilitation, smoking cessation support (Quitline 13 78 48 and pharmacotherapy), and review of blood pressure and lipid management.

part2.lead: Here are Phillip's observations from the practice nurse and the 12-lead ECG she has just recorded.
part2.patient:
Phillip is still in pain (8/10, or 6/10 if GTN was given in Part 1). Put these to the candidate when they explain the plan, if they have not already covered them:

  • "Is this a heart attack? Am I going to die?"
  • "The hospital's only ten minutes away. Can't Margaret just drive me? I don't want a fuss with an ambulance." Agree to the ambulance once the candidate explains that his heart rhythm could become dangerous on the way and the paramedics can treat it and get him straight to the right team.
  • "What will they do to me at the hospital?"

handover.label: Observations
handover.result: Taken by the practice nurse with Phillip on the couch, on room air. No observation chart in the clinic.
handover.model:
Read: heart rate 96, rising to 104 at the repeat set; blood pressure 152/90 mmHg right and 148/88 mmHg left (a 4 mmHg difference, well under the 20 mmHg that would raise concern for dissection), then 144/86 mmHg (systolic 132 mmHg if GTN was given in Part 1); respiratory rate 20 then 22; SpO2 97% then 96% on room air; temperature 36.7 °C; BGL 6.4 mmol/L; pain 8/10 (6/10 if GTN given), not relieved.

For Phillip: not shocked and not hypoxic. The rising heart rate and respiratory rate with unrelieved pain show he is getting worse without treatment. Equal arm pressures argue against aortic dissection. Systolic pressure well above 90 mmHg means GTN is safe (with no phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor).

What it changes: no oxygen (SpO2 not below 93%); GTN and opioid analgesia can be given; continuous monitoring and repeat observations every few minutes until the paramedics arrive.

rows.note: On arrival, right arm, on the couch. Pale and sweaty.
Repeat set after ECG recorded; still sweaty. If GTN was given in Part 1, the examiner reads pain as 6/10 and SBP 132 mmHg at 14:20.

handover.label: 12-lead ECG (with ECG from 2 years ago)
handover.result:
12-lead ECG, resting, recorded at 14:12 in the practice. Clinical details: 60-year-old man, central chest pain for 50 minutes.

  • Rate: 98 beats/min.
  • Rhythm: sinus rhythm.
  • Axis: +20°.
  • PR interval: 164 ms. No PR depression.
  • QRS: 94 ms. No bundle branch block. No pathological Q waves.
  • QT: 340 ms, QTc 435 ms (Bazett).
  • ST segments: ST elevation in V1 (1.5 mm), V2 (4 mm), V3 (4 mm), V4 (3 mm), V5 (2 mm), I (1 mm) and aVL (1.5 mm). ST depression in III (1.5 mm) and aVF (1 mm), and 0.5 mm in II.
  • T waves: tall, broad-based (hyperacute) T waves in V2 to V4.
  • Other: no left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria.
  • Comparison: ECG from 2 years ago (routine blood pressure review): sinus rhythm at 70 beats/min, normal axis, normal ST segments and T waves. The ST and T changes are new.

Conclusion: sinus rhythm with new ST elevation in the anterior and lateral leads (V1 to V5, I, aVL) and reciprocal inferior ST depression, meeting criteria for acute ST-elevation myocardial infarction.
handover.model:
Read: sinus rhythm at 98, normal axis, PR, QRS and QTc. ST elevation of 4 mm in V2 and V3 (the criterion for a man aged 40 or over is at least 2 mm) and at least 1 mm in two or more neighbouring leads elsewhere (V4, V5, I, aVL). Reciprocal ST depression in III and aVF, hyperacute T waves in V2 to V4, no Q waves yet, no bundle branch block. New compared with the ECG from 2 years ago.

For Phillip: acute anterolateral STEMI, most likely a proximal left anterior descending artery occlusion: a large area of myocardium at risk. Reciprocal change and the territorial pattern make pericarditis unlikely. No Q waves and 50 minutes of pain mean there is still myocardium to save.

What it changes: a time-critical emergency. Call 000 now, give aspirin 300 mg and GTN, insert IV access, give titrated analgesia, monitor with the defibrillator ready (risk of ventricular fibrillation), and arrange reperfusion: primary PCI or fibrinolysis. Send the ECG and the old ECG with the paramedics. Do not wait for a troponin.

ask: What do his observations and his ECG show?
What is the most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider?
The ECG shows he is having an acute myocardial infarction. What is your management of Phillip, here in the clinic and afterwards?
What will you tell Phillip, and what safety netting and follow-up will you arrange?

guide:
In Part 1 the examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they are examining. If the candidate starts to measure the respiratory rate or temperature, stop them and give the values (as the original station directs). If they ask for the ECG, or acknowledge that the nurse is recording it and ask to see it as soon as it is done, say the nurse is recording it and it will come in Part 2; credit item 22. Management items done in Part 1 count in Part 2: if, from the history, the candidate calls 000 or gives aspirin or GTN during Part 1, credit those Management items when they occur and do not ask for them again. If GTN was given in Part 1, read the 14:20 pain as 6/10 and systolic BP as 132 mmHg. The additional examination (lungs, abdomen, lower limbs) earns item 21 if it is done or clearly stated, even without time to perform it. In Part 2 hand over both results together and ask the questions in order. Phillip puts his questions while the candidate explains the plan. For oxygen (item 31), accept either threshold: below 93% (NHFA/CSANZ) or below 90% (ESC).

A high-performing candidate sees straight away that Phillip is unwell. They take a brisk, targeted chest pain history that covers dissection, PE, the contraindications to aspirin and GTN, and the crescendo exertional symptoms. They complete a systematic cardiovascular examination that looks for dissection (both arm pressures, pulse deficits, an aortic regurgitation murmur) and for complications (crackles, S3, new murmur), and ask for the ECG at once. In Part 2 they read the ECG systematically, name an anterolateral STEMI, call 000 at once, give aspirin 300 mg and GTN after checking blood pressure and PDE5 inhibitor use, withhold oxygen at 97%, place IV access, titrate opioid, stay with Phillip with the defibrillator ready, and explain the plan and reperfusion honestly.

A borderline candidate performs a routine examination without linking it to the chest pain, asks for the ECG only at the end, or gives the drugs but lets Margaret drive him to hospital, sends him to ED by private car or tells him to make his own way, or waits for a troponin. Failing to recognise the setting and call 000 is a fail on Management, as in the original marking criteria.
explain:
The diagnosis: acute anterolateral STEMI

Phillip has 45 minutes of heavy, crushing central chest pain at rest, radiating to the left arm and jaw, with sweating, nausea and breathlessness. He has major risk factors (age, male sex, 30 pack-years of smoking, hypertension, hypercholesterolaemia) and two weeks of new exertional chest tightness, a crescendo prodrome. The ECG shows new ST elevation in V1 to V5, I and aVL with reciprocal depression in III and aVF: an acute anterolateral ST-elevation myocardial infarction, most likely from a proximal left anterior descending artery occlusion.

Approach to acute chest pain in general practice

Anyone with possible acute coronary syndrome should have a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of first medical contact. The ECG is the test that sorts STEMI, which needs immediate reperfusion, from the rest. A normal ECG does not exclude ACS. Point-of-care or laboratory troponin must never delay transfer. People with chest pain should call 000 rather than drive or be driven, because ventricular fibrillation is most likely early in infarction and paramedics can defibrillate and start treatment on the way.

What the cardiovascular examination adds

  • Dissection: an inter-arm blood pressure difference, pulse deficits, radio-femoral delay, an early diastolic murmur of aortic regurgitation, neurological signs. All are absent here. This matters because antiplatelet, anticoagulant and fibrinolytic treatment can be catastrophic in dissection.
  • Complications of infarction: hypotension and cool peripheries (cardiogenic shock), crackles, an S3 and a raised JVP (heart failure; Phillip is Killip class I), a new pansystolic murmur (papillary muscle rupture or ventricular septal rupture), a rub.
  • Risk factor stigmata: tar staining, corneal arcus, xanthelasma, tendon xanthomata (familial hypercholesterolaemia), obesity.
  • Other findings in the routine examination (endocarditis stigmata, Marfan and Turner features, malar flush, Argyll Robertson pupils, high-arched palate) are part of the full cardiovascular examination and should be looked for, even though they are normal here.

Interpreting the results

Observations: heart rate rising into mild tachycardia while in pain, blood pressure well above 90 mmHg systolic with equal arms, normal oxygen saturation, afebrile. He is not shocked or hypoxic, so GTN is safe and oxygen is not needed.

ECG: STEMI criteria are new ST elevation at the J point in two neighbouring leads of at least 1 mm, except in V2 and V3, where the threshold is at least 2 mm in men aged 40 or over (2.5 mm under 40) and 1.5 mm in women. LBBB (new or not) with ongoing ischaemic symptoms is managed as a STEMI equivalent. Reciprocal depression supports infarction over pericarditis. Pericarditis gives widespread concave ST elevation with PR depression and no reciprocal change apart from aVR (and sometimes V1).

Immediate management in the clinic

  • Call 000 and state the ECG diagnosis. This is the most important step in the original marking scheme.
  • Aspirin 300 mg orally, chewed or dissolved, unless he has a true allergy.
  • GTN sublingual spray, 1 to 2 sprays (400 to 800 micrograms), repeated every 5 minutes if pain continues, up to 3 doses, while systolic BP stays at least 90 mmHg. Do not give if systolic BP is below 90 mmHg, if he has taken a phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor (sildenafil or vardenafil within 24 hours, tadalafil within 48 hours) or if right ventricular infarction is suspected.
  • Oxygen only if hypoxic: SpO2 below 93% (NHFA/CSANZ 2016; ESC uses 90%). Routine oxygen is not recommended when saturation is 93% or above.
  • IV access: two large-bore cannulae.
  • Analgesia for severe pain that continues: morphine 2.5 to 5 mg IV every 5 to 10 minutes or fentanyl 25 to 50 micrograms IV every 5 to 10 minutes, titrated to effect.
  • Monitoring: stay with him, repeat the observations, keep the defibrillator attached or beside him and follow ANZCOR basic and advanced life support if he arrests.

Definitive care

For STEMI within 12 hours of symptom onset, the Heart Foundation and CSANZ guideline recommends reperfusion. Primary PCI is preferred when it can be delivered promptly. Otherwise fibrinolysis is given, by paramedics before hospital in some regions or at the nearest hospital, followed by transfer to a PCI centre. The ECG sent ahead by paramedics often lets the catheter laboratory be activated directly. The second antiplatelet agent and anticoagulation are chosen by the receiving team according to the reperfusion strategy.

Safety netting and follow-up

While he waits, Phillip should report worsening pain, breathlessness, faintness or palpitations at once, and staff must be ready to start CPR and defibrillate. After discharge he needs a written heart attack action plan: rest and use GTN, and call 000 if symptoms are severe, get worse quickly or last more than 10 minutes. Follow-up includes GP review with the discharge summary, cardiac rehabilitation, smoking cessation (the most powerful change he can make; Quitline 13 78 48 and pharmacotherapy), and secondary prevention medicines and risk factor targets as set by his cardiologist.
points: Acute chest pain needs a 12-lead ECG within 10 minutes of first medical contact. Do not finish a long examination first.
STEMI: new ST elevation in two neighbouring leads (at least 2 mm in V2 and V3 in men aged 40 or over, 1 mm elsewhere), with reciprocal depression supporting infarction over pericarditis.
STEMI in general practice: call 000 and never send the patient by private car or wait for a troponin.

Immediate treatment: aspirin 300 mg, GTN if systolic BP is at least 90 mmHg and no PDE5 inhibitor has been taken, oxygen only if hypoxic, two IV cannulae, titrated IV morphine or fentanyl, and a defibrillator at the bedside.

In chest pain, the cardiovascular examination looks for aortic dissection (arm pressures, pulse deficits, aortic regurgitation), complications (heart failure, new murmur, shock) and risk factor stigmata.
STEMI within 12 hours needs reperfusion (primary PCI, or fibrinolysis if PCI cannot be delivered in time), then cardiac rehabilitation, smoking cessation and a heart attack action plan.
